articles.title: Dragons – Definition: A Study by N. Politis
articles.excerpt: Analytical study on the folk conception of dragons as transformed serpents with anthropomorphic characteristics and erotic behavior.

content.value: M. Hatzopulos, "Parnassos" vol. XV p. 59. It is difficult to distinguish the dragon as imagined by those who recount the tradition — whether as a serpent, or as an anthropomorphic giant or Orion. This ambiguous image is preserved in other narratives about dragons, both Greek and from other peoples. This stems from the common depiction of dragons as large and powerful serpents, who have the power to transform into humans, usually maintaining human form. This is connected to the erotic obsession of dragons, who took women as lovers.

John of Damascus mentions that in his time such beliefs about dragons prevailed. The tradition states: “Dragons transform into human form, while sometimes the serpents become small and other times very large, surpassing the size and bulk of the human body. There are also descriptions of dragons who transform into humans and mingle with people, seizing women and coupling with them.”

The dragon in this tradition is presented as someone who sucks the blood of his lover. This episode is similar to a story from a Lesbian fairy tale, in which the Devil, transformed into a two-headed serpent, sucks the blood of his wife.
Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, N. G. Politis – Traditions, Part B, 1904 – p. 967

articles.title: Dragon-Wolves of Thesprotia – Narrative of Saint John the Evangelist
articles.description: Dragon-Wolves of Thesprotia – Narrative of Saint John the Evangelist
articles.excerpt: Historical narrative of Saint John the Evangelist and his exorcistic confrontation with the demon-wolf in Thesprotia.

content.value: According to a communication by T. Zerledis (1855). For the holy dragon-slayers, see the following entry. The Synaxarion of Saint John the Evangelist recounts how the Saint expelled a demon from the island, who appeared as a wolf, to whom twelve people were offered as victims each month. The Synaxarion is contained in codex no. 4922 of our Pouniki Library (f. 9ʹ 26ʹ, written in 1545). At the beginning of this text the following narrative about the wolf is given:

“Concerning a wolf who appeared to the inhabitants of the city as a wolf: this was an unclean demon. When we arrived in the city, no one recognized us. It was during the month of which we speak, and when we arrived at a place called Iastirion, there were the leading men of the city, holding twelve small children bound in chains and laid upon the ground. John therefore asked one of those present at that place, saying: ‘What is the reason for these bound children?’ The man replied: ‘During this month of which we speak, twelve small children are held and offered as sacrifice to the beneficent wolf.’ John asked: ‘And who is this wolf? I too would wish to know.’ The man replied: ‘Around the fourth hour of the day, the priests come and take the children and lead them as a sacrifice to the wolf; and great multitudes of people follow. If you too wish to follow, you will see the wolf and the sacrifice made to it.’ John said to the man: ‘Friend, I see you are adorned, yet since you are a stranger, how might I see the wolf?’ The man replied: ‘He appears both to strangers and to locals, to everyone.’ John said: ‘Come, let us go to that place, for I wish to see him. And if you show him to me, I will give you a priceless pearl, whose worth is second to nothing.’
“Only show me the wolf, for I long to see him.” Hearing these words, the man went with eagerness to John to show him the place and reveal the wolf to him.

And when they came to the place (f. 956b), the man said to John: “Here, we have arrived at the place. Give me the pearl and I will show you the wolf.” John said to him: “Friend, do not doubt, but show me the wolf, and take the pearl.”

When John had said this to the man, suddenly the spirit called “wolf” appeared and was ascending the river. And John said to it: “I tell you, evil spirit, hear me.” Immediately the spirit halted. And John said to it: “How many years have you been in this place?” And the spirit replied: “I have been here sixty years.” And John said to it: “In the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, depart from this place.” Immediately the evil spirit vanished from our sight. And the man, seeing this, fell at the feet of John and worshipped him, saying: “Mercy, man of God, tell me who you are and whence you come, for you perform these miracles.” And John replied to him: “I am a disciple of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. That which you call wolf and evil spirit is the spirit of the devil, which destroys the souls of men. For this reason Christ sent me here, to drive out the spirits and to preach the truth to men.”

The man, hearing this, fell upon his face and worshipped him again, saying: “Man of Christ, make me also to become of Christ.” And John, having read from the Holy Scriptures, taught him concerning the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. And again he fell at the feet of John and besought him: “I beg you, give me the seal of Christ.” When John went to the river, he baptized him in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

When we had come up from the river, John said to the man: “See, you have received the priceless pearl.” And while John was speaking to the man, there came some who were defiled, holding twelve children who had been bound, to deliver them to the demon who accompanied them.

When they drew near to the river, at the place where they completed their ritual for the demon, they appeared to be in a trance, filled with fear and trembling, and began to slaughter the children. When therefore these men arrived at the spot and bound the children and took up their knives, they continued their act in accordance with the commands of the demon, to slaughter the children. John, drawing near, said to them: “Men, you who do not know the way of truth and follow the demon known by the name of wolf — Jesus Christ, the Son of God, I have driven him from this place. Therefore your labors in this place are in vain. Release the children and I will announce to you how to save your souls and these children.” When the men heard the words of John, they all stood astonished and no one dared to give an answer at that moment. They said among themselves that the wolf who had forced the river to flow had brought them to ruin.

John said to them again: “I told you to release the children and let them go. The spirit you are awaiting, the demon, I have driven from this place by the power of my God.” And there was no reply from the defiled.

John, drawing near, loosed the bonds of the children and said to them: “Go to the city, to your fathers, mothers, and brothers.” None of their own people followed. And again, John, drawing near, took the knives from the hands of the defiled, and all stood astonished. No one dared to resist.”
John spoke sternly, saying that they had hindered him, and they all entered the city.

John stood in a place where there was a small portico called a “thyra” (gate), and many people gathered there. When John had read from the sacred texts, he began to teach them concerning the Son of God. And some believed him, while others did not. He also explained the cause of the demon called “wolf.”

All the people were persuaded and gave thanks to John for the life he had granted them, for the miracles performed for the children. The sinners began to draw away from John and were unwilling to hear his word.
Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, N. G. Politis – Traditions, Part B, 1904 – pp. 968–972

articles.title: Kefalonia – Legend of 2 Brothers – Dragon-Slayers
articles.excerpt: Historical account of the slaying of a dragon at the fortress of Saint George by the Vreskanos brothers in 1509.

content.value: This summary refers to a report written in May 1509 and registered in the Kefalonia archives. The report was published by Ainos, who observes that the folk tradition is confirmed by this account, with the difference that it mentions two brothers of unknown origin, rather than the family to which the forest belongs.

The two brothers, Iakovos and Vernardos Vreskanos, slew the terrible dragon at the fortress of Saint George in Kefalonia. They used iron armor and, after one brother thrust his sword into the dragon’s mouth, the other struck it with an axe. The battle was fierce and lasted for several moments, with the dragon resisting using its tail.

The report also mentions the enormous size of the dragon, the burning of its body in front of the church, and the holding of a public thanksgiving service for their success in slaying the dragon. The two brothers were rewarded with a fief for their deed. The date of the event was 10 May 1509.
Studies on the Life and Language of the Greek People, N. G. Politis – Traditions, Part B, 1904 – pp. 977–978

articles.title: The Dragon of Koumaria
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Dramatic folk narrative of the mythical dragon of Koumaria and its tragic encounter with humans

content.value: In the deep ravine of Koumaria, near Arachova, there once dwelt a terrible dragon. One day it drew a man toward itself from afar with its breath. When the wretched man had been swallowed up to his armpits, he stretched out his arms and cried out for help.

Many saw him from afar, and one of them, wishing to end his suffering quickly, called out: “Pull in your arms and the dragon will let you go!” The wretched man did as he was told, and immediately the dragon swallowed him whole.

articles.title: The Drakolakkos – Syros
articles.author: Νικόλαος Γ. Πολίτης
articles.excerpt: Narrative of the mythical dragon of Syros and its tragic confrontation

content.value: At the foot of the northern hills, on the western shores of Syros, facing the village of Galisas, there is a very deep cave called Drakolakkos. In it lurked a terrible dragon; sometimes it stayed in the cave, other times it came down to a spot called Katafya, where it rested beneath a fig tree on the estate of Leonardos Damoflis. When the dragon was at Katafya, no one dared to pass along the road nearby.

One day, however — it was a Friday — a man looked carefully at that spot, saw that the beast was gone, and sent his son with the donkey to bring firewood to his house at Apano Syra, so that his wife could heat the oven and bake bread.

The poor child went as his father had instructed, but as he was passing through Katafya, at that very moment the dragon came down from its cave and leapt upon him and devoured him, and the animal returned empty to Apano Syra.

The father grew suspicious and ran at once to that place; he saw blood and understood the calamity that had befallen him. He then gathered many of his friends and they lay in wait for the dragon, and when it was returning to its cave, they fell upon it and finished it off with their axes.

The father walked ahead of the others, to avenge his child’s blood, but since he was poisoned by the creature’s breath, and since it had also wounded him, he died within two days. From the stench that came from the slain beast, for a long time no one could pass along that road.

articles.title: The Dragons at Agios Isidoros of Rhodes
articles.author: Αναστάσιος Βρόντης
articles.excerpt: Legend of a stone marked with dragons’ fingerprints at Agios Isidoros of Rhodes (Atreia), where dragons tested their courage. Whichever dragon managed to move the great stone became their leader.

content.value: At Ay Siero (Agios Isidoros) there is a large stone with the dragons’ fingerprints on it, and this place was formerly called Atreia because dragons came there to test how brave they were. Whichever dragon managed to move the great stone became their leader.

articles.title: The 3 Dragons of Rhodes
articles.author: Αναστάσιος Βρόντης
articles.excerpt: Legend of three dragons of Rhodes (Koumouri, Filerimos, Paradisi) who threw a stone to one another. The dragon of Paradisi let it fall near Maritsa, where the spot is called “At the Stone”.

content.value:
In the old days it was said that three dragons lived on Rhodes. One at Koumouli (Koumouri), another at Filierimo (Filerimos), and the third at Paradisi. The dragon of Koumouli picked up a stone and threw it onto Filerimos. The dragon of Filerimos in turn threw it to Paradisi.

The dragon of Paradisi wanted to throw it back to Koumouli but did not, and instead let it fall from the mountain near Maritsa.

From then on, the place where the stone fell was called “At the Stone”, and whoever passes by there can see a large stone.
